paper.title_en: Little Red Dots as Shock-Powered High-Energy Neutrino Sources
paper.abstract_en: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact, high-redshift sources whose physical nature remains uncertain. Their optical spectra motivate a scenario in which their emission may be powered by shocks interacting with dense surrounding material. We investigate whether such interactions can power LRDs and contribute to the diffuse high-energy neutrino intensity measured by IceCube. In our simplified model, a fast central-engine outflow drives a shock through stationary or slow outflowing material, followed by a prescribed quasi-stationary interaction near the LRD photosphere. We consider the time-averaged neutrino emission from shock-active LRDs without requiring a single shock to persist throughout the LRD lifetime. We explore parameter ranges motivated by the observed and inferred properties of LRDs, finding solutions with shock luminosities 2.0e43 < L_s < 3.5e44 erg/s. Using an analytical framework for cosmic-ray acceleration and hadronic interactions in dense shock environments, we calculate the resulting high-energy neutrino emission and integrate it over the cosmological LRD population. For our fiducial cosmic-ray parameters, the average predicted contribution below 2e5 GeV increases from 0.2% for the lowest-luminosity quintile to 2% for the highest-luminosity quintile, while an illustrative higher-efficiency case reaches 13% of the IceCube diffuse neutrino intensity. These estimates assume all observed LRDs are shock-active. A smaller active fraction or a reduced covering factor would decrease the predicted intensity, whereas survey incompleteness could increase it. Improved models and population synthesis are needed to constrain the total LRD contribution.
